notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 25, drawn from the sources I was able to access:

---

## Overview / Structure

**Authorship and Occasion:** David is the author. Spurgeon styles it "the second of the seven Penitential Psalms" and suggests it comes from his later days — the period of Absalom’s rebellion — because he mentions "the sins of my youth" and his many foes. "It is the mark of a true saint that his sorrows remind him of his sins, and his sorrow for sin drives him to his God." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

**Acrostic Structure:** This is the first alphabetical (acrostic) psalm, with each verse beginning with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet — though not perfectly. Gill notes the Jews themselves confess ignorance as to the reason, though it may help memory. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm) Guzik (Enduring Word) adds three likely purposes: literary beauty, a sense of completeness (A to Z), and aid to memorization. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

**Twofold Mood:** Spurgeon divides the psalm into alternating prayer and meditation: vv. 1–7 prayer; vv. 8–10 meditation; v. 11 prayer; vv. 12–15 meditation; vv. 16–22 prayer. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: *"To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul."*

The phrase is an expressive figure of surrender. Guzik: "It was as if David held his soul in outstretched hands up to heaven saying, 'Here I am LORD, completely surrendered unto you.'" Maclaren (quoted by Guzik) notes: "The very nature of such aspiration after God demands that it shall be exclusive." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Gill offers three possible interpretations: (a) in prayer — denoting sincere, affectionate, hearty prayer; (b) as an offering — presenting the soul as a living sacrifice; (c) as a "depositum" — committing the soul into God's care and protection, as in Psalm 31:5. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary emphasizes the Hebrew phrase means "a permanent setting of the affections on him," not a temporary raising of the heart (citing Deuteronomy 24:15). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/25.htm)

Spurgeon: "True prayer may be described as the soul rising from earth to have fellowship with heaven; it is taking a journey upon Jacob's ladder, leaving our cares and fears at the foot, and meeting with a covenant God at the top." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

### v. 2: *"in You, my God, I trust. Do not let me be put to shame; do not let my enemies exult over me."*

Spurgeon notes the progression from "LORD" (v. 1) to "my God" — "the sweet singer has drawn nearer to his heavenly helper … 'My God!' It is … more than celestial music." Faith is "the cable which binds our boat to the shore." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Guzik: David speaks partly to himself, assuring himself of his trust and the expected reward — not to be ashamed before God or enemies. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Wesley defines "ashamed" succinctly: "Disappointed of my hope." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 3: *"Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame; but those who are faithless without cause will be disgraced."*

Guzik stresses that "waits on You" is not passive but active service — like a waiter attending to every need of the one being served. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "This is not a petition … but an affirmation of confidence." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

The biblical idea of "ashamed" here, says Boice (via Guzik), is not primarily embarrassment but "being let down or disappointed or of having trusted in something that in the end proves unworthy of our trust" — as in Romans 5:5 and Isaiah 49:23. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Spurgeon sees David's heart enlarged by suffering: "If we pray eagerly for ourselves, we shall not long be able to forget our fellow sufferers." "Prayer when it is of the Holy Ghost's teaching is never selfish." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Gill interprets "transgress without cause" as acting treacherously without just reason — David's subjects who rebelled though he ruled righteously. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

**Honor–Shame Reading (Wesleyan/Methodist):** Timothy and Julie Tennent (Seedbed, Asbury Seminary) note: "Western cultures have typically emphasized the forensic or legal side of Christ's work … However, from the time of the fall … we discover three great effects of sin: guilt, shame, and fear." Psalm 25 focuses on shame, not guilt. "Guilt and innocence can be declared in private as we repent quietly in the presence of God. But shame and honor are about our life in the world — the public testimony of those around us." (https://wakeupcall.seedbed.com/episodes/let-me-not-be-ashamed-psalm-25)

### v. 4: *"Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths."*

The Pulpit Commentary calls this "an echo of the prayer of Moses when his people were rebellious at Sinai (Exodus 33:13)," repeated by David in Psalm 27:11 and 86:11. Man is "so morally blind and ignorant, that, unless enlightened from on high, he cannot discern aright the 'way of godliness.'" It then quotes Newman's hymn: "Lead, kindly Light … I do not ask to see the distant scene; one step enough for me." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/25.htm)

Guzik: David longed for public vindication but was not haughty — if he needed guidance or correction, he wanted God to give it *before* any public humiliation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Gill notes the dual sense: God's own ways in creation, providence, and grace — and the paths God appoints for His people to walk in. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

Wesley: "Teach me my duty, and cause me to keep close to it, notwithstanding all temptations." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 5: *"Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation; all day long I wait for You."*

Guzik notes we can be sure that no one taught by God in His paths has been led into sin or compromise that produces public disgrace. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

The Pulpit Commentary: "'Thy truth' would seem to mean here 'the true, right path' — the 'way of godliness.'" The prayer has two parts — teach the psalmist the path *and* lead him in it, i.e., cause him to walk in it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/25.htm)

Gill: "Lead me in thy truth" refers to the Word of God, the Scriptures of truth, and the Gospel. He wants God to lead him by His Spirit more and more into all truth. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

"Four times over in these two verses he applies for a scholarship in the college of grace." (Spurgeon) (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** In his sermon on Psalm 25, John Piper emphasizes that David prays about his confusion. "If you face a decision, and there is no biblical command relating directly to that specific choice, should you wait for a dream or a vision or a voice in your head? … It seems to me that the Bible describes the ordinary guidance of God as the development of spiritual sensitivity … the prerequisite of divine guidance is not the quest for messages, but the quest for holiness." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-goodness-of-god-and-the-guidance-of-sinners)

### v. 6: *"Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and loving devotion, for they are from age to age."*

Guzik breaks down the Hebrew: "tender mercies" = *racham racham* (repetition for intensity — "compassionate compassions"); "lovingkindness" = *hesed* (God's deep covenant love, in the plural — as if God's covenant love was so great it couldn't be thought of in the singular). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Spurgeon says "from of old" should more correctly be translated "from eternity." "David was a sound believer in the doctrine of God's eternal love. The Lord's loving-kindnesses are no novelties." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Gill: The petition is for a "fresh discovery and application of the grace, mercy, and loving kindness of God," not that God has actually forgotten. The love of God is "from everlasting … to everlasting, and remains invariably the same." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 7: *"Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts; remember me according to Your loving devotion, because of Your goodness, O LORD."*

Spurgeon: "Sin is the stumbling block. This is the thing to be removed." "Those offences which we remember with repentance God forgets, but if we forget them, justice will bring them forth to punishment." "He who presumes upon his youth is poisoning his old age." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Guzik: Immediately after asking God to *remember* (v. 6), David asks God to *forget*. He wanted God to forget his youthful sins (in the sense of forgiving them). "When God remembers his mercy, he forgets our sins" (Horne, quoted in Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Gill sees this as confessing sin "from his youth upwards unto that time, as in Jeremiah 3:25." He notes David's "more notorious and glaring" sins — murder and adultery in the matter of Uriah and Bathsheba — and that the rebellion of Absalom was the chastening foretold in 2 Samuel 12:11. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: "An earthly father does not remember them against his son. How much less will our heavenly Father!" David asks to be remembered "in the light of thy tender mercy, with the rays of thy love streaming over me and hiding the deformities of my transgressions." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 8: *"Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way."*

Guzik: David learned this "through love more than logic" — it would be just as logical for a good and upright God to destroy sinners. Yet God's goodness benefits sinners instead of destroying them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Wesley: God is "Holy and true, in all his declarations and offers of mercy to sinners. Therefore — He will not be wanting to such poor sinners as I am, but will guide them into the way of life and peace." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

Spurgeon: "Here the goodness and rectitude of the divine character are beheld in friendly union; he who would see them thus united … must stand at the foot of the cross and view them blended in the sacrifice of the Lord Jesus." "What a ragged school is this for God to teach in!" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Gill: God teaches sinners "by his word and Spirit the evil of their ways, and bring them out of them … and he will teach them his own ways, both the ways and methods of his grace, in saving sinners by Christ." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 9: *"He guides the humble in what is right and teaches them His way."*

The Pulpit Commentary: "It is only such sinners as are 'meek' — i.e., humble, submissive, contrite, teachable — that God will take in hand and teach. The proud and perverse he will leave to their own devices." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/25.htm)

Spurgeon: "Meek spirits are in high favour with the Father of the meek and lowly Jesus, for he sees in them the image of his only-begotten Son." "Proud of their own wisdom fools will not learn, and therefore miss their road to heaven, but lowly hearts sit at Jesu's feet." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Gill: "The meek" can also be rendered "the miserable" — those who see themselves as wretched, lost, and undone, who cry out, "What shall we do to be saved?" God leads them "gently; see Jeremiah 10:24; into every truth of the Gospel by degrees, and as they are able to bear them." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** "A person who admits his sinfulness, and feels helpless in himself has one of the indispensable spiritual qualifications for discerning what pleases the Lord. The quest for guidance must be the quest for humility." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-goodness-of-god-and-the-guidance-of-sinners)

### v. 10: *"All the LORD's ways are loving and faithful to those who keep His covenant and His decrees."*

Guzik: This is not a feel-good platitude but a tested conviction. The condition is staying in God's covenant and word. He quotes Spurgeon's vivid image: "In the Hebrew I find the word here used is 'wheel tracks,' such ruts as wagons make when they go down our green roads in wet weather and sink in up to the axles. God's ways are at times like heavy wagon-tracks, and they cut deep into our souls; yet they are all of them mercy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

The Pulpit Commentary: "Mercy and truth will meet together (Psalm 85:10) in the case of those who, however they may have sinned, meekly submit themselves to God's guidance, and thenceforth keep his covenant and his testimonies." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/25.htm)

Spurgeon: "This is a rule without exception … There shall be mercy in every unsavoury morsel, and faithfulness in every bitter drop." "Keepers of the covenant shall be kept by the covenant." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Gill clarifies that "paths of the LORD" here means God's own paths — His counsels, purposes, covenant, and steps in Christ — all of which are mercy and truth to His people. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 11: *"For the sake of Your name, O LORD, forgive my iniquity, for it is great."*

Guzik: "It is strange (but true) spiritual logic: *pardon my iniquity, for it is great.* We can only imagine a criminal in a court of law appealing to the judge on this basis." David knew that he was a great sinner, but God is an even greater Savior. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Spurgeon: "This sentence of prayer would seem out of place were it not that prayer is always in its place, whether in season or out of season." "The logic of faith … is clean contrary to that of a legal spirit; faith looks not for merit in the creature, but hath regard to the goodness of the Creator." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Gill: David prays that God would "mercifully pardon" or "be propitious" — through the propitiation of Christ. The argument "for it is great" may seem backwards, but it denotes "the sense the psalmist has of his iniquity, and his importunity for the pardon of it; just as a person, sensible of the violence and malignity of his disease, entreats the physician with the greater eagerness." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

Wesley: "For — Or, *though* (as this particle is often rendered) it be great. Possibly he speaks of his sin against Uriah and Bathsheba." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: "God's perfections of love, mercy, goodness, and truth are manifested (his name …) in pardoning sin, and the greatness of sin renders pardon more needed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 12: *"Who is the man who fears the LORD? He will instruct him in the path chosen for him."*

Spurgeon: "Let the question provoke self examination. Gospel privileges are not for every pretender. Art thou of the seed royal or no?" "If we make our will God's will, God will let us have our will. God does not violate our will, but leaves much to our choice; nevertheless, he instructs our wills, and so we choose that which is well pleasing in his sight." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Guzik notes the Hebrew poetic device of repetition: humility (v. 9) is set next to reverent fear of God (v. 12) — the two concepts are closely connected. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Gill: "the way that he shall choose" can mean either the way the God-fearer chooses (the way of truth and duty, Psalm 119:30) or the way God prescribes. "A great happiness it is for a man to have his steps ordered by the Lord and his goings directed by him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

Wesley: "Chuse — Which God appointeth." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 13: *"His soul will dwell in prosperity, and his descendants will inherit the land."*

Guzik sees this as David speaking in faith — though his present situation was bad, he trusted that prosperity and blessing would come. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Gill: "His soul shall dwell at ease, or in 'goodness' … enjoying an affluence of good things, of spiritual blessings in Christ … at death, when his soul is separated from his body, it shall enter into rest, and be in perfect peace." The "seed" inheriting the earth points forward to the new heavens and new earth (Matthew 5:5), the millennium, and ultimate glory. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

Spurgeon: "He who fears God has nothing else to fear … It is not abundance but content that gives true ease." "God remembers Isaac for the sake of Abraham, and Jacob for the sake of Isaac." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Wesley: "At ease — Heb. in Good; in the possession and enjoyment of the true good. The land — Canaan; which was given as an earnest of the whole Covenant of Grace, and all its promises." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 14: *"The LORD confides in those who fear Him, and reveals His covenant to them."*

This is one of the most commented-upon verses in the psalm.

Guzik: "The secret of the LORD" (*sod*) means intimate fellowship known only by those who fear and obey God — a reality the spiritually dead cannot grasp (1 Corinthians 2:14). VanGemeren: "The Hebrew idiom … may here be translated by 'intimate circle' (cf. Job 19:19; 29:4; Proverbs 3:32). Those who do his will are his confidants, as was Abraham (Genesis 18:17)." Spurgeon: "Some read it 'the friendship:' it signifies familiar intercourse, confidential intimacy, and select fellowship." Maclaren: "Whether we translate the first word 'secret' or 'friendship,' the sense is substantially the same." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Spurgeon: "The higher spiritual life is necessarily a path which the eagle's eye hath not known, and which the lion's whelp has not travelled … Saints have the key of heaven's hieroglyphics; they can unriddle celestial enigmas." "He who does not know the meaning of this verse, will never learn it from a commentary; let him look to the cross, for the secret lies there." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Precept Austin expands: "The Hebrew word *sod* … can also mean counsel or council." The secret "is divine. It is supernatural. It is available only from Jehovah, the Sole Possessor … made intelligible to the hearts of natural men and women who are in Christ." The prerequisite is the fear of the LORD — a conscious, deliberate choice (*bachar*), "not impulsively." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-2514-15-commentary)

Wesley: "The secret — His love and favour, which is called his secret, Job 29:4, Prov 3:32, because it is known to none but him that enjoyeth it." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 15: *"My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh."*

Guzik: David said this both as a statement of fact and a prayer for the future. His feet were still in the net his enemies set against him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Spurgeon: "Observe the conflicting condition in which a gracious soul may be placed, his eyes are in heaven and yet his feet are sometimes in a net." "Though our feet are in the net, if our eyes are up unto God, mercy certainly will interpose." He notes "pluck" is a rough word — "the Lord plucks at us sharply to let us feel that sin is an exceeding bitter thing." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

Precept Austin: "Looking to the Lord is an expression of faith in the Lord's power to deliver … David looks to Jehovah Who never ceases to look at us." It also warns believers will encounter many snares from the world, flesh, and devil. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-2514-15-commentary)

Wesley: "Pluck — He will deliver me out of all my troubles." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 16: *"Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted."*

Guzik notes the "clever turn of thought": in v. 15 David had turned his attention toward the LORD; here he asks God to turn His attention toward His needy servant. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Spurgeon: "His own eyes were fixed upon God, but he feared that the Lord had averted his face from him in anger. Oftentimes unbelief suggests that God has turned his back upon us." "Saints still must stand upon the footing of mercy; notwithstanding all their experience they cannot get beyond the publican's prayer, 'Have mercy upon me.'" "He was lonely and bowed down." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Identifies loneliness as one of the four struggles David brings to God in this psalm — alongside fear, guilt, and confusion. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-goodness-of-god-and-the-guidance-of-sinners)

### v. 17: *"The troubles of my heart increase; free me from my distress."*

Guzik observes that "this sweet, comforting psalm came from a season of agony for David." He quotes 2 Corinthians 4:8–10 as Paul's parallel: "hard pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

### v. 18: *"Consider my affliction and trouble, and take away all my sins."*

Guzik: "It was as if David recognized, 'I have many enemies and troubles, but none greater than my own sins. Please God, deal also with all my sins.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

### vv. 19–20: *"Consider my enemies … Guard my soul and deliver me; let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in You."*

Guzik: David's present difficulty would not prevent him from trusting and serving God. "This was a deep relationship with God, not one easily damaged or separated by disappointment." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Wesley: on v. 20, "Soul — My life." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 21: *"May integrity and uprightness preserve me, because I wait for You."*

The Pulpit Commentary notes David scarcely means his own inherent integrity (which he has just confessed is lacking — "my iniquity is great," v. 11). Rather, it is "an integrity and uprightness whereto he hopes to attain, by the grace of God, in days to come — an integrity and uprightness for which he 'waits.'" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/25.htm)

### v. 22: *"Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress."*

This verse stands outside the acrostic pattern (the Hebrew letter *tav* is not used), which some take as evidence it was added later — perhaps during the Exile. The Pulpit Commentary notes that David was "not a slave to a mechanical arrangement," and the similar irregularity at the end of Psalm 34 argues against a late addition. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/25.htm)

Guzik: "David had a deep concern for the blessing and welfare of God's people as a whole, not merely himself … One of the worst aspects of difficulty and trial … is that it can lead one to become terribly self-focused." David's humility prevented that. Poole (quoted): "If thou will not pity and help me, yet spare thy people, who suffer for my sake, and in my sufferings." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

Gill sees a messianic reach: David "may have a further view to the redemption of the church of God, the spiritual Israel, by the Messiah … to redeem his people from all their iniquities; from the law, its curses and condemnation … and from death itself, the last enemy, which will put an end to all their troubles, Isaiah 35:10." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/25.htm)

Wesley: "If thou wilt not help me, yet spare thy people who suffer for my sake, and in my sufferings." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/25.htm)

---

## Protestant Traditions: Points of Emphasis

### Reformed / Reformed Baptist (Piper, Desiring God)
John Piper's sermon on Psalm 25 stresses that divine guidance comes not through seeking special messages, dreams, or visions but through the development of "spiritual sensitivity" — a heart and mind brought into harmony with God's character through Scripture. He identifies four prerequisites for guidance: (1) admitting sin, (2) humility, (3) covenant-keeping / fearing God, and (4) faith. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-goodness-of-god-and-the-guidance-of-sinners)

### Methodist / Wesleyan (Wesley, Seedbed/Tennent)
Wesley's notes are characteristically brief and practical, focusing on the moral-spiritual meaning. The Tennents (Seedbed, Asbury Theological Seminary) bring a distinctive honor–shame lens: "Western cultures have typically emphasized the forensic or legal side of Christ's work … However, from the time of the fall … we discover three great effects of sin: guilt, shame, and fear." In Psalm 25, "David does not focus on his guilt but his shame." Public vindication — being honored before the watching world — is central to the psalm's cry. (https://wakeupcall.seedbed.com/episodes/let-me-not-be-ashamed-psalm-25)

### Baptist (Spurgeon)
Spurgeon reads the psalm Christologically throughout — the union of goodness and uprightness in v. 8 is seen "at the foot of the cross." He emphasizes the doctrines of grace: eternal love (v. 6), effectual calling, covenant theology (v. 10, 14). His notes are rich in experiential application — the believer's felt sense of sin, the "rough" plucking from the net, the "secret" fellowship with Christ. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps025.php)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik (Calvary Chapel tradition) reads the psalm with emphasis on personal devotion, surrender, and active waiting upon God. He stresses the emotive and relational dimensions — David "held his soul in outstretched hands," God's covenant love is so great "it could not be thought of in the singular." The commentary is broadly evangelical, focusing on application to the believer's prayer life in seasons of trouble. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-25/)

---

## What I Could Not Find

I was unable to access the following within my search and fetch limits:

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings** (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) — e.g., whether the Church Fathers read v. 22 as a prophecy of Christ's redemption or how the "secret of the LORD" relates to sacramental theology
- **Lutheran perspectives** (lcms.org, 1517.org) — e.g., the Law/Gospel hermeneutic applied to the psalm's confession-pardon dynamic
- **Modern scholarly notes** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) — e.g., discussion of the acrostic irregularities, textual variants, or the psalm's place in the Psalter's editorial structure
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-grace readings** — none of the accessible sources engaged with how these traditions might handle v. 13 ("his soul will dwell in prosperity") or the conditional promises of v. 10
- **Precept Austin's full verse-by-verse** — only vv. 14–15 had dedicated commentary
